explanations.explanation: I see why that one tempts you, friend, since angels have been all over this letter. But the writer says, “For it is not to angels that He has subjected the world to come…” (Hebrews 2:5). So the world to come is not put under angels. The text says it plainly, so I'll say it plainly too.
That's right, baker. The writer says, “For it is not to angels that He has subjected the world to come…” (Hebrews 2:5). It's a flat no on the angels. The world to come is not put under them.

Yes, friend. The psalm says, “You made him a little lower than the angels…” (Hebrews 2:7). A LITTLE lower, not a lot lower. And look at what comes next: “You crowned him with glory and honor” (Hebrews 2:7).

I get why you'd hesitate, but the quote says it straight: “You made him a little lower than the angels…” (Hebrews 2:7). So God did make man a little lower than the angels. That part is true. It also goes right on to say that He crowned him with glory and honor.

Nothing, baker! The writer says, “When God subjected all things to him, He left nothing outside of his control.” (Hebrews 2:8). Not one thing got left off the list. That's about as thorough as a baker who checks every single oven twice.

The sea sounds like a big enough thing to be left out, I'll give you that. But the writer never names it here. He says, “…He left nothing outside of his control.” (Hebrews 2:8). Nothing means nothing, friend, sea included.

Big thinking, friend, but the writer doesn't name the heavens as the leftover. He says, “…He left nothing outside of his control.” (Hebrews 2:8). That doesn't leave a loose corner for anything. The word is nothing, and I'm sticking to it.

True, and the writer is honest about it. He says, “Yet at present we do not see everything subject to him.” (Hebrews 2:8). He doesn't pretend otherwise. Neither will I. My own bakery doesn't always listen to me either.

I see why it's tempting after that big line about everything being put under man. But the very next words are, “Yet at present we do not see everything subject to him.” (Hebrews 2:8). So the writer is saying that right now we DON'T see it.

That's the one, baker. The writer says Jesus is “…now crowned with glory and honor because He suffered death…” (Hebrews 2:9). The reason is right there in the verse. This is a heavy part, so I'll let those words sit for a second.

Angels are all over this stretch of the letter, so I see why you picked it. But the writer's reason is different: Jesus is “…now crowned with glory and honor because He suffered death…” (Hebrews 2:9). Commanding the angels is not the reason he gives. This is a heavy part, friend, so it's worth reading that verse slowly.

A crown and a conquering army do go together in a lot of stories, friend. But the writer gives a different reason: Jesus is “…now crowned with glory and honor because He suffered death…” (Hebrews 2:9). Conquered nations don't show up in this verse at all. This is a heavy part, so take your time with it.
Many sons, baker. The writer says God is “…bringing many sons to glory…” (Hebrews 2:10). Jesus is the author of their salvation, and God is the one bringing them. Many, friend. Not a small batch.

Elders are a fine group, but they aren't who the writer names. He says God is “…bringing many sons to glory…” (Hebrews 2:10). The verse says sons, and it doesn't sort anyone by office. Let's stick to what the verse says.
That's a very specific guess, friend, and I respect the commitment. But the verse doesn't mention Levites. It says God is “…bringing many sons to glory…” (Hebrews 2:10). Sons is the word on the page.

Suffering, baker. The writer says it was fitting for God “…to make the author of their salvation perfect through suffering.” (Hebrews 2:10). That's a heavy line, and I think it deserves a quiet moment. It's the word the verse uses, and we can trust it.

Miracles sound like the more exciting answer, I know. But the verse says God made Jesus “…perfect through suffering.” (Hebrews 2:10). That's the word the writer picked, and it's a heavy one. I think it's worth reading again slowly.

Victory is a strong word, friend, but it's not the one in this verse. The writer says God made the author of salvation “…perfect through suffering.” (Hebrews 2:10). That's a heavy line to sit with. I think it's worth a second read.

Yes, friend. The writer says, “For both the One who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are of the same family.” (Hebrews 2:11). So Jesus and the people He sanctifies belong to one family. Same family. No awkward introductions needed at the door.

I can see why you'd doubt it, since it's a big claim. But the writer says it outright: “For both the One who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are of the same family.” (Hebrews 2:11). So it's true. Jesus and the people He sanctifies are family.

Brothers, baker! The verse says, “So Jesus is not ashamed to call them brothers.” (Hebrews 2:11). Jesus and the people He sanctifies are one family, so He calls them brothers. Not ashamed. I'd put that on a tea towel, but my mustache can't sew.

Servants is a fair guess, since people often think of it that way. But the verse says, “So Jesus is not ashamed to call them brothers.” (Hebrews 2:11). Brothers is the word, friend. That's family talk, not job talk.

I see where you were headed, but strangers is the opposite of what the verse says. It says, “So Jesus is not ashamed to call them brothers.” (Hebrews 2:11). Same family, so no strangers here. Not even the ones who show up empty-handed at the cookie table.

God's name, friend. In this quote, Jesus speaks to God, and He says, “I will proclaim Your name to My brothers…” (Hebrews 2:12). The name is what He says He'll proclaim. I think that's a sweet thing to promise His brothers.

Law is a common thing to expect in the Bible, I know. But in this quote Jesus is speaking to God, and He says, “I will proclaim Your name to My brothers…” (Hebrews 2:12). The word is name, friend. Law isn't in that line.

Covenant is a weighty word, so I see why it came to mind. But in this quote Jesus is speaking to God, and He says, “I will proclaim Your name to My brothers…” (Hebrews 2:12). It's name, not covenant. The verse keeps it simple.

That's the one, baker. The writer says Jesus shared in our humanity so that by His death He might destroy “…him who holds the power of death, that is, the devil…” (Hebrews 2:14). The writer names him outright. So there's no guessing about who it is.
Herod was a king in the Gospels (Matthew 2:1), so I see why he came to mind. But he isn't named here. The writer says the one who holds the power of death is “the devil.” (Hebrews 2:14).
Goliath was a giant from Gath (1 Samuel 17:4), so I see why he came to mind. But he's not in this passage. The writer names “the devil” as the one who holds the power of death. (Hebrews 2:14).

Death, baker. The verse says Jesus would “…free those who all their lives were held in slavery by their fear of death.” (Hebrews 2:15). All their lives, friend. I think a fear that long would feel heavy to carry.

Judgment is a weighty word, I know. But the verse says the slavery was by “…their fear of death.” (Hebrews 2:15). So that's the fear the writer names. I think it's worth noticing how it describes them: all their lives.
Rulers can make people nervous, no doubt. But the verse says the slavery was by “…their fear of death.” (Hebrews 2:15). That's the fear on the page. Rulers don't come up in that line.

I get why it sounds right, because angels are all through this letter. But verse 16 says, “For surely it is not the angels He helps, but the descendants of Abraham.” (Hebrews 2:16). So it's the descendants of Abraham He helps, not the angels.
That's right, friend. The writer says, “For surely it is not the angels He helps, but the descendants of Abraham.” (Hebrews 2:16). Angels are great, but they aren't who this verse says He helps.

A high priest, baker. The verse says Jesus was made like His brothers so “…He might become a merciful and faithful high priest in service to God…” (Hebrews 2:17). Merciful and faithful, both together. That's two good words right in a row.

Prophet is a fair guess, friend, since the Bible is full of them. But the verse says Jesus became “…a merciful and faithful high priest in service to God…” (Hebrews 2:17). High priest is the title the writer picks here. It's the one that goes with making atonement.

A king is easy to picture, I know. But the verse says Jesus became “…a merciful and faithful high priest in service to God…” (Hebrews 2:17). The writer picks high priest, friend. That's the title in the verse, so that's the one I'm baking with.

Yes, baker. The writer says, “Because He Himself suffered when He was tempted, He is able to help those who are being tempted.” (Hebrews 2:18). Jesus knows what it's like. I think that's a good thing to hold onto on a rough day.

I see why you thought of them. But verse 16 already said it's not the angels He helps, and verse 18 says He is able to help “…those who are being tempted.” (Hebrews 2:18). The angels who sinned aren't in this passage. The ones He helps are the tempted.

Priests fit with the high priest talk, so I get the thinking. But the verse says Jesus is able to help “…those who are being tempted.” (Hebrews 2:18). The priests of Levi don't come up here. That tempted group is whoever needs the help, friend.
